chief_complaint: 6-month history of recurrent fever, night sweats, and progressive back pain.
history_of_present_illness: A 33-year-old male refugee presented with a 6-month history of recurrent fever, night sweats and progressive back pain. He started feeling ill in a refugee camp in Iran about 6 months ago and was treated with tablets and intragluteal injections, leading to temporary symptom subsidence, but symptoms recurred after treatment ended. His family reached Germany 4 months ago, and all medical documents were lost during the journey.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a 33-year-old male refugee from Afghanistan, who lived in a refugee camp in Iran before reaching Germany 4 months ago, after crossing Turkey and Eastern Europe. Spinal brucellosis may be common or predominant in highly endemic countries such as Afghanistan.
vitals: Vital signs are normal, and the patient is afebrile.
physical_exam: The patient is in fair general condition. Examination revealed marked spinal tenderness in the lumbar region, with the remaining examination being unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: Differential blood count, liver and renal function tests, and LDH were normal. C-reactive protein was 26 mg/L (<5 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 40 mm/hour (<20 mm/hour), both slightly raised. Urinalysis was unremarkable. MRI of the spine revealed signal enhancement of the L3 and L4 vertebral bodies, the corresponding vertebral disc, and the right psoas muscle, as well as disc space narrowing and irregularities of both adjacent vertebral endplates. A chest x-ray showed no abnormalities. Several blood cultures and sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli were negative. A CT-guided biopsy of the lesion was performed, and culture of the tissue sample revealed Brucella melitensis. No additional sites of infection were identified on imaging, and there was no sign of endocarditis on echocardiography.
differential_diagnosis: The most likely differential diagnoses for infectious spondylitis in this febrile young adult included tuberculosis, which is globally the main cause of infectious spondylitis. Spinal brucellosis was also considered highly probable given the patient's origin from Afghanistan, a highly endemic country. Other infectious causes of spondylitis were considered, mirroring osteomyelitis, typically following hematogenous spread from a distant site of infection, including pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus, pyogenic and non-pyogenic streptococci, Gram-negative bacteria such as Salmonella species, histoplasmosis, actinomycosis, and melioidosis, depending on local epidemiology.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient's condition was classified as complicated brucellosis with spondylitis and para-vertebral abscess formation. He was treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampicin 900 mg daily for 16 weeks, along with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g daily for the first 3 weeks. Fever subsided within several days, and inflammation parameters normalized weeks after therapy initiation. A second MRI at the end of treatment showed complete resolution of the paravertebral abscess, and he remained relapse-free one year post-treatment.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was complicated brucellosis, caused by Brucella melitensis. This was confirmed by the culture of the tissue sample obtained via CT-guided vertebral biopsy. The diagnosis was supported by the patient's history of recurrent fever, night sweats, and back pain, his refugee status from Afghanistan (an endemic region), physical examination findings of localized lumbar spinal tenderness, and MRI imaging demonstrating spondylodiscitis of L3/L4 with psoas muscle involvement. The patient showed a positive clinical and radiological response to specific antimicrobial combination therapy.
